# Chicken Kabsa 🇸🇦

::: {.dish-meta}
**Region:** Saudi Arabia & the Arabian Peninsula  ·  **Family:** One-pot pilaf
**Serves:** 4–6  ·  **Active time:** 45 minutes  ·  **Total:** 1 hour 15 min
:::

*Kabsa* is the great communal rice dish of the Gulf — a mound of spiced
long-grain rice cooked in aromatic chicken broth, the bird piled on top, meant to
be shared from a single platter. It is the taste of Saudi hospitality.

## The story

Kabsa (*kabsah*) is the national dish of Saudi Arabia and a close relative of
dishes found across the Peninsula and into Yemen (where *mandi* is cooked in a
tandoor-like pit oven). Its defining flavor comes from a warm, slightly citrusy
spice blend and, above all, from **loomi** — dried limes — which lend a haunting,
fermented sourness you can't get any other way. The rice is cooked directly in
the spiced stock, absorbing everything.

## Ingredients

**Aromatics & chicken**

- 1 whole chicken (~1.5 kg), in 4–8 pieces
- 2 tbsp oil (or plant-based butter, in place of ghee)
- 2 large onions, finely chopped
- 6 cloves garlic, minced; 1 tbsp grated ginger
- 3 tomatoes, grated or finely chopped (or 400 g canned)
- 2 tbsp tomato paste

**Kabsa spice (baharat-style blend)**

- 1 tsp each: ground cumin, coriander, black pepper
- ½ tsp each: ground cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, nutmeg
- 1 tsp paprika, ½ tsp turmeric
- Whole: 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 2 bay leaves
- **2 dried limes (loomi), pierced** — the signature note
- Pinch of saffron or a little more turmeric for color

**Rice**

- 400 g (2 cups) basmati rice, rinsed and soaked 20 min
- ~1 L (4 cups) chicken stock or water
- Salt

**To finish:** toasted almonds and pine nuts, raisins fried in a little oil, fresh
parsley; serve with *daqqus* (a fresh tomato-chili sauce)

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Gluten-free · dairy-free:** naturally gluten-free (rice, whole spices, dried
lime). The only dairy is ghee — swapped here for **oil or plant-based butter**.
Use a certified GF stock or bouillon if you're not using homemade.
:::

## Method

1. In a large heavy pot, brown the chicken pieces in the oil until golden on all
   sides. Remove and set aside.
2. In the same pot, cook the onions until soft and lightly golden, 6–8 minutes.
   Add garlic and ginger, then all the whole and ground spices. Bloom, stirring,
   1–2 minutes until fragrant.
3. Add the tomatoes and tomato paste; cook down 5 minutes into a thick, jammy
   base.
4. Return the chicken and add the stock and the **pierced dried limes**. Season
   with salt. Bring to a boil, cover, and simmer 25–30 minutes until the chicken
   is tender. Lift the chicken out and keep warm.
5. Taste the broth — it should be well seasoned and tangy from the loomi. Add the
   drained rice directly to the broth. There should be about 1.5× the rice's
   volume in liquid; top up with hot stock if needed.
6. Bring back to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat 15 minutes.
   Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat.
7. For a traditional finish, brush the chicken with a little oil or melted plant
   butter and **broil or grill it a few minutes** until the skin crisps and colors.
8. Fluff the rice onto a large platter, pile the chicken on top, and shower with
   fried nuts, raisins, and parsley. Serve with daqqus on the side.

## The loomi difference

Dried limes are non-negotiable for real kabsa. Pierce them so the broth can pull
out their sour, almost smoky perfume; fish them out (or warn guests) before
serving, as they're intensely bitter to bite. Find them at any Middle Eastern
grocer, whole or ground.

## Make it yours

- **Mandi:** the chicken is smoked or oven-finished over the rice for a
  barbecue-like aroma — drop a piece of hot charcoal in a foil cup into the pot,
  cover, and let it smoke for 5 minutes.
- **Mathbi / madfoon** are grilled and buried variants across the Peninsula.
- Bump the heat with fresh green chili in the base, or keep it gentle and let the
  daqqus sauce do the spicing at the table.
